summary.text: A 39-year-old left-handed man with untreated hypertension and alcohol and tobacco use developed a thunderclap headache with sudden neurological deficit, vision loss, left-sided weakness and seizures. He was evaluated at the NINN, where subarachnoid and frontal and parietal hemorrhages and a right middle cerebral artery aneurysm were identified.

After early treatment he developed vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia with bilateral occipital hemorrhagic infarctions. Ventricular derivation was later performed, followed by more severe left leg weakness and hyperactive delirium; deficits improved with treatment and rehabilitation, but complete visual loss was present before discharge and treatment continued as an outpatient.

At home he tripped, had difficulty finding his way, denied his vision loss and voiced delusions of being dead. Examination showed confabulation and impaired judgment with intact alertness, attention, speech and language; later he became agitated and aggressive and required hospitalization. Neuro-ophthalmology found loss of all visual sensation with preserved pupillary reflexes and bilateral vitreous hemorrhage consistent with Terson syndrome.

Imaging showed bleeding with a right frontal hematoma and, two months after the initial hemorrhage, infarction with secondary hemorrhage of the occipito-parietal and occipital lobes; neurocognitive assessment found deficits in orientation, memory and executive function. The authors diagnose Anton and Cotard syndromes; with clozapine and valproate most symptoms responded, but visual anosognosia and confabulations persisted.
